lessons.title: Experiments with RND
intro: A simulation lets the computer try something thousands of times, like rolling a die, and count what happens. Scientists at Dartmouth used this to study chance.
The pattern: a FOR loop for the experiments, RND for each random event, and a counter for the results you're interested in.
The output changes every run, because the dice are random. The output below is just one possible run. But the more often you repeat the experiment, the closer the result gets to the true chance.

exercises.prompt: About how many sixes do you expect in 600 rolls?
exercises.explanation: A six comes up in 1 of 6 rolls on average, and 600 / 6 = 100. The real count will be close, but rarely exactly 100.

exercises.prompt: Why does the example print a different number every time?
options: RND produces new random rolls on every run
The loop counts differently each time
exercises.explanation: That's what makes it a simulation: every run is a new experiment.

exercises.prompt: You run the experiment with 60,000 rolls instead of 600. What changes?
options: The share of sixes gets closer to exactly 1 in 6
exercises.explanation: With more experiments, random ups and downs even out. This is called the law of large numbers.

exercises.prompt: Simulate a coin: K should be 0 or 1.
exercises.explanation: 2 * RND(1) is between 0 and 1.99…, and INT turns that into 0 or 1.

exercises.prompt: This always prints 0 or 1 instead of about 100. Which line is in the wrong place?
exercises.explanation: The counter is reset to 0 in every round. LET C = 0 belongs before the loop.

exercises.prompt: What's the chance of rolling a 6 with one die?
exercises.explanation: A die has six equally likely sides, and one of them is the 6.

lessons.title: All Possibilities
intro: Sometimes you don't need chance at all. Two dice only have 6 × 6 = 36 possible results, so the computer can simply try every one of them.
Two nested loops go through all combinations: A for the first die, B for the second. Counting the ones you're interested in gives the exact answer.
This always gives the same result. Simulations are for problems with too many possibilities to try them all.

exercises.prompt: How many combinations do two dice have?
exercises.explanation: Each of the 6 values of the first die can meet each of the 6 values of the second: 6 × 6 = 36.

exercises.prompt: In how many ways can two dice add up to 12?
exercises.explanation: Only 6 + 6. That's why 12 is so rare, while 7 has six different ways.

exercises.prompt: Count the doubles (both dice show the same number).
exercises.explanation: Skip the counting when the dice are different. Only doubles reach line 50, and there are 6 of them.

exercises.prompt: What's the chance of rolling a 7 with two dice?
exercises.explanation: 6 of the 36 combinations add up to 7, and 6/36 = 1/6.
It counts sums of 10 or more: 10 three ways, 11 two ways, 12 one way. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

exercises.prompt: When do you need a simulation instead of trying all possibilities?
options: When there are far too many possibilities to try them all
exercises.explanation: Two dice are easy to try out completely. A card game with millions of possible deals is not, so you simulate.

lessons.title: Counting with Lists
intro: To count every possible result at once, use a list as a row of counters: S(2) counts the rolls that sum to 2, S(3) those that sum to 3, and so on.
LET S(A + B) = S(A + B) + 1 adds one to exactly the right counter. Afterwards, a loop prints the whole table.
The same idea works for simulations: roll randomly, then add one to the counter of whatever came up.

exercises.prompt: Why use a list S instead of separate variables?
options: The sum itself picks the counter, so one line counts every result
exercises.explanation: S(A + B) automatically points to the right counter. With separate variables, you'd need an IF for every sum.

exercises.prompt: After the example has run, what is S(7)?
exercises.explanation: Six combinations add up to 7, so the counter for 7 was increased six times.

exercises.prompt: Which sum of two dice is the most common?
exercises.explanation: 7 has six ways, more than any other sum. That's why it plays a special role in many dice games.

exercises.prompt: Count one more for this sum.
exercises.explanation: The counter for this sum goes up by one.

exercises.prompt: This stops with ?INDEX 11 OUT OF RANGE. Which line has to change?
exercises.explanation: Sums go up to 12, but the list only has room up to 10. It needs DIM S(12).

exercises.prompt: You roll one die 600 times and count with LET S(D) = S(D) + 1. What do you expect in S(1) to S(6)?
exercises.explanation: Each side is equally likely, so each counter ends up near 100, but rarely exactly.
